title: Why AI Sales Can’t Stop at the Close
gist: BCG argues that for engineered AI products (configurable agents, workflow-transforming systems, customized deployments) revenue is won through post-signature consumption, not at the close, so the SaaS bookings funnel must become a use-case flywheel with forecasting by workload, continuous technical ownership across pre- and post-sales, and incentives tied to adoption and expansion. Supporting signals: 51% of CROs report greater demand for customized proof of value, Gartner found at least half of generative AI projects were dropped after proof of concept by end-2025, and vendors experimenting with five-year terms are shifting risk from renewal into underconsumption.

themes.theme: From bookings funnel to consumption flywheel

insights.claim: For complex AI products, revenue is increasingly driven by consumption and value is co-produced with customers who must change their processes, data and ways of working, so the SaaS go-to-market logic of converting qualified demand into contracts (a funnel) gives way to converting use cases into sustained consumption (a cycle).
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Bookings, RPO and billings become weaker leading indicators for AI software vendors; weight consumption and use-case expansion metrics more heavily in valuation.
insights.quote: The first is naturally a funnel. The second is naturally a cycle.
insights.locator: Introduction

insights.claim: Two AI accounts can sign similar contracts and look equally healthy in the pipeline, yet months later one has moved to its third use case while the other still cannot get its first into sustained use; their revenue trajectories diverge long before renewal and a bookings-centric commercial system may not detect it.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Expect delayed, lumpy net-revenue-retention surprises at AI vendors whose reporting is bookings-centric; ask managements for cohort consumption data, not just ACV.
insights.locator: Introduction

insights.claim: The commercial shift is not uniform: embedded copilots and task-automation features can still be sold much like SaaS modules, while engineered AI products — configurable agents, workflow-transforming systems and customized deployments — require a go-to-market reset with new structures and roles.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Segment AI software exposure by product complexity: copilot-style add-ons keep SaaS-like margins and sales efficiency, while agentic/engineered products carry heavier services cost and consumption risk.
insights.locator: Introduction

insights.claim: For engineered AI, the decisive evidence at renewal accumulates over months of usage and realized outcomes, making contract signature merely one moment in the commercial relationship rather than the point where the sale is won.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Closing-velocity metrics overstate AI vendor health; realized-usage and outcome data are the true renewal predictors.
insights.quote: Increasingly, signature is merely one moment in the commercial relationship rather than where the sale is won.
insights.locator: The Funnel Becomes a Flywheel

insights.claim: AI account economics should be forecast by workload rather than deal value, using use-case pipeline, consumption velocity and expansion potential, because deal value alone says little about how much of an AI product will ultimately be used.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Look for AI vendors disclosing consumption velocity and use-cases-per-account; those metrics better predict revenue than contract value.
insights.quote: Account economics increasingly need to be forecast by workload.
insights.locator: The Funnel Becomes a Flywheel

insights.claim: Complex AI vendors that stop at technical delivery cap their own expansion potential, which is pulling them into work that once sat with the customer or a systems integrator — workflow integration, decision rights, change support and adoption.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Second-order competitive threat to IT services firms and systems integrators as AI vendors internalize deployment and change work; also a margin headwind for vendors doing it.
insights.locator: The Funnel Becomes a Flywheel

themes.theme: Buyer proof demands and pilot attrition

insights.claim: A BCG CRO survey found 51% of chief revenue officers report greater demand for customized proof of value reflecting the buyer's own data, processes and environments, pushing the burden of proof earlier in the AI sales process.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Longer, costlier pre-sales cycles for AI vendors — a drag on sales efficiency (magic number, CAC payback) that favors vendors with domain-specific proof assets.
insights.quote: 51% of CROs report greater demand for customized proof of value
insights.locator: Six Shifts Are Rewriting the Sale of AI Products

insights.claim: Gartner found that by the end of 2025 at least half of generative AI projects had been dropped after proof of concept, often due to poor data quality, inadequate risk controls, escalating costs or unclear business value.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: High POC attrition means AI pipeline conversion assumptions should be haircut; vendors helping clear data-quality and governance hurdles capture disproportionate share.
insights.quote: at least half of generative AI projects had been dropped after proof of concept
insights.locator: The Funnel Becomes a Flywheel

insights.claim: A successful AI demo can prove the technology works without creating conviction that it will work in the customer's environment, and production then exposes data, integration, governance and process constraints that a pilot can sidestep.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Pilot counts are a poor proxy for AI revenue; track pilot-to-production conversion as the key signal.
insights.locator: The Funnel Becomes a Flywheel

insights.claim: Because AI products evolve faster than customers can evaluate them, AI sellers must narrow the field in discovery by helping pick a use case worth pursuing and defining sufficient proof, and in complex domains industry credibility becomes the price of admission since the judgment depends on understanding the workflow, not just the product.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Favors vertical, domain-credible AI vendors over horizontal model-centric sellers in complex enterprise workflows.
insights.locator: Six Shifts Are Rewriting the Sale of AI Products

insights.claim: Some enterprises are funding new AI purchases by reallocating budget away from other vendors, so incumbent application providers and AI-native vendors increasingly compete for the same dollar; whether AI budgets stay centralized or migrate back into application budgets is still unclear.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: AI spend is partly a zero-sum wallet-share shift, a risk for incumbent application SaaS seat revenue; watch for budget cannibalization commentary in enterprise software earnings.
insights.quote: Incumbent application providers and AI-native vendors can therefore find themselves competing for the same dollar.
insights.locator: Six Shifts Are Rewriting the Sale of AI Products

insights.claim: Buyer appetite for open-ended strategy-first AI selling (maturity assessments, broad strategy exercises) is fading in favor of bounded, testable formats such as time-bound bootcamps, value-discovery exercises and pilots that give a clearer path to a product decision.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Headwind for pure AI strategy consulting revenue; demand shifts toward execution-linked, outcome-bounded engagements.
insights.locator: Six Shifts Are Rewriting the Sale of AI Products

insights.claim: In AI sales the account executive becomes a value architect who sequences use cases and orchestrates a cross-functional pod, while AI itself absorbs more sourcing, qualification and routine outreach, pushing the role toward judgment-heavy work.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Lower-tier SDR/qualification headcount is exposed to automation while senior AE and solution roles gain value; relevant to sales-tech vendors and staffing models.
insights.quote: The account executive becomes a value architect.
insights.locator: The Commercial Organization Moves Beyond the Close

insights.claim: The boundary between pre-sales and post-sales engineering is dissolving because proof, deployment and adoption rely on the same accumulated understanding of customer data and workflows, giving rise to roles such as forward-deployed engineers, deployment strategists and AI outcome managers.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Forward-deployed engineering headcount is becoming a structural cost line for AI vendors, weighing on gross margins versus classic SaaS.
insights.locator: The Commercial Organization Moves Beyond the Close

insights.claim: A clean handoff between pre-sales and post-sales can discard the context needed to move a promising AI pilot into production, and deployment engineers are often the first to spot the next value-creation opportunity, so continuity of technical ownership matters more than titles.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Vendors with continuous engineer-per-account coverage should show better pilot-to-production and expansion rates; handoff-heavy org designs are a red flag.
insights.locator: The Commercial Organization Moves Beyond the Close

insights.claim: Customer success in AI is bifurcating, with generalist coverage supplemented by technical and domain experts, and professional services has become a strategic battleground where many vendors subsidize value discovery, bootcamps and even the first pilot, monetizing later through scaled accelerators, center-of-excellence support or advanced engineering.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Subsidized front-end services depress near-term AI vendor margins; scrutinize services gross margin and whether later monetization actually materializes.
insights.locator: The Commercial Organization Moves Beyond the Close

insights.claim: Applying one commercial model across all AI products makes simple products unnecessarily expensive to sell while leaving complex ones without enough support to reach sustained consumption, and a specialist-heavy motion that works for the largest strategic accounts may be unaffordable beyond them.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: High-touch AI deployment economics may not scale down-market; question mid-market growth assumptions for agentic AI vendors.
insights.locator: The Commercial Organization Moves Beyond the Close

insights.claim: Some AI vendors are exploring longer commercial commitments including five-year terms and extended price protection, but fewer renewal decisions do not remove commercial risk; more of it shifts into underconsumption over the life of the contract.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Long-dated AI commitments inflate RPO without guaranteeing realized revenue; underconsumption against committed contracts is the hidden risk to model.
insights.quote: More of it shifts into underconsumption over the life of the contract.
insights.locator: The Commercial Organization Moves Beyond the Close

insights.claim: In consumption-driven AI sales, AEs need incentives to grow the total customer relationship and technical and product specialists need credit for the adoption, consumption and expansion they materially influence, with consumption signals feeding directly into forecasting, account reviews and resource allocation.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Comp-plan redesign toward consumption credit is an observable indicator that an AI vendor is operationally ready for usage-based revenue.
insights.locator: The Commercial Organization Moves Beyond the Close

themes.theme: Early client lessons on operating the flywheel

insights.claim: Existing commercial systems cannot reliably measure AI usage or surface it to sellers, so vendors need consumption tracking by customer and use case piped directly into CRM and account-management workflows; without it commercial teams are flying blind.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Demand signal for usage-metering, billing and revenue-intelligence tooling integrated with CRM as AI vendors retool.
insights.quote: Until that capability is in place, commercial teams are effectively flying blind.
insights.locator: Four Lessons from Early Client Work

insights.claim: Sellers at enterprise software companies need a clear reason to prioritize new AI offerings over established products; leading organizations create that conviction by anchoring the pitch in a specific customer problem, arming sellers with measurable-impact evidence and aligning incentives to reward adoption of the new product.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Slow AI attach at incumbent software firms may reflect seller incentive misalignment rather than weak product; watch for comp changes as a catalyst.
insights.locator: Four Lessons from Early Client Work

insights.claim: No single function owns the AI consumption flywheel; a practical start is mapping stages from deployment through adoption, the capabilities needed at each, clear ownership across sales, customer success, services and technical teams, and where role continuity is critical.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Diagnostic for judging AI vendor execution: ask who is accountable when contracted capacity fails to become consumption.
insights.quote: No one function owns the flywheel
insights.locator: Four Lessons from Early Client Work

insights.claim: The talent gap in selling and activating AI is proving as important as the operating-model gap, forcing explicit build-versus-hire choices against a defined capability map.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Scarce AI deployment and domain talent is a binding constraint on AI vendor growth and a source of wage inflation in go-to-market roles.
insights.quote: The talent gap is proving as important as the operating-model gap.
insights.locator: Four Lessons from Early Client Work

themes.theme: CRO stress test and open questions

insights.claim: A CRO can stress-test an AI commercial model by stripping bookings out and asking where revenue would rise or disappear if it reflected only what customers actually consumed, exposing where contracted value is turning into consumption and where it is stalling.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Investors can apply the same lens: re-underwrite AI vendors on consumed revenue rather than bookings to spot where committed value may evaporate.
insights.quote: Strip bookings out of the picture.
insights.locator: The Hard Questions Come Next

insights.claim: Deciding which AI products, use cases and segments warrant the intensive flywheel motion versus a conventional sales motion could turn on value at stake, technical complexity, customer readiness, regulatory burden or a combination, and how much high-touch support is affordable for strategic accounts versus the broader enterprise base remains unresolved.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: Commercial model for agentic AI is not settled; expect experimentation and margin volatility in AI vendor go-to-market spend.
insights.locator: The Hard Questions Come Next

insights.claim: The AI vendors that first master a consumption-based commercial model will set the rules the rest of the market must follow, even though the playbook for selling AI products is still under development.
insights.speaker: Federico Fabbri
insights.so_what: First-mover advantage in consumption-led go-to-market is a potential durable edge; favor AI vendors already reporting and managing to consumption.
insights.quote: The vendors who figure out this consumption model first will force the rest of the market to play by their rules.
insights.locator: The Hard Questions Come Next
